paragraphs: Some of my readers may imagine that my young man was a sickly, ecstatic, underdeveloped creature, a pale, consumptive dreamer. On the contrary, Alyosha at this time was a well-built, red-cheeked, clear-eyed lad of nineteen, glowing with health. He was very handsome, too: graceful, moderately tall, with dark brown hair and a regular, rather long, oval face. His dark gray eyes were wide-set and shining. He was very thoughtful and seemed very serene. I will be told, perhaps, that red cheeks do not rule out fanaticism and mysticism. But I think Alyosha was more of a realist than anyone. Oh, no doubt in the monastery he fully believed in miracles, but to my mind miracles never trouble a realist. It is not miracles that lead realists to belief. The true realist, if he is an unbeliever, will always find the strength and the ability to disbelieve in the miraculous. If he is faced with a miracle as an undeniable fact, he would sooner doubt his own senses than accept the fact. Even if he accepts it, he accepts it as a fact of nature that he had not recognized until then. In the realist, faith does not spring from the miracle; the miracle springs from faith. Once the realist believes, his very realism obliges him to admit the miraculous too. The Apostle Thomas said that he would not believe until he saw, but when he did see, he said, “My Lord and my God!” Was it the miracle that forced him to believe? Most likely not. He believed only because he wanted to believe, and perhaps he fully believed in his secret heart even when he said, “I do not believe till I see.”

I will be told, perhaps, that Alyosha was stupid, undeveloped, had not finished his studies, and so on. It is true that he did not finish his studies, but to call him stupid or dull would be a great injustice. I will simply repeat what I said above. He took this path only because at that time it alone struck his imagination and offered his soul an ideal way out of darkness and into light. Add to that that he was to some extent a youth of our last epoch—that is, honest by nature, wanting the truth, seeking it and believing in it, and wanting to serve it at once with all the strength of his soul; he looked for immediate action and was ready to sacrifice everything for it, even life itself. These young men unfortunately fail to understand that sacrificing one’s life is, in many cases, the easiest of all sacrifices. They do not see that giving up, say, five or six years of their seething youth to hard and tedious study—if only to multiply tenfold their power to serve the truth and the cause they have set as their goal—is a sacrifice utterly beyond the strength of many of them. The path Alyosha chose ran in the opposite direction, but he chose it with the same thirst for swift achievement. As soon as he thought seriously, he was convinced that God and immortality exist, and at once he said to himself, instinctively: “I want to live for immortality, and I will accept no compromise.” In the same way, if he had decided that God and immortality did not exist, he would at once have become an atheist and a socialist. For socialism is not merely the labor question; it is above all the atheistic question, the question of the form atheism takes today, the question of the tower of Babel built without God, not to climb from earth to heaven but to bring heaven down to earth. Alyosha would have found it strange and impossible to go on living as before. It is written: “Give all that thou hast to the poor and follow Me, if thou wouldst be perfect.”

Alyosha said to himself: “I can’t give two roubles instead of ‘all,’ and only go to mass instead of ‘following Him.’” Perhaps his childhood memories brought him to our monastery, where his mother may have taken him to mass. Perhaps the slanting sunlight and the holy image that his poor “crazy” mother had held him up to still worked on his imagination. Brooding on these things, he may have come to us only to see whether here he could sacrifice everything, or only “two roubles.” And in the monastery he met this elder. I must digress to explain what an “elder” is in Russian monasteries, and I am sorry to say I do not feel very competent to do so. I will try, however, to give a superficial account of it in a few words. Authorities on the subject assert that the institution of “elders” is of recent date, not more than a hundred years old in our monasteries, though in the Orthodox East, especially on Sinai and Athos, it has existed for over a thousand years. It is maintained that it existed in ancient times in Russia too, but through the calamities that befell Russia—the Tartars, civil war, the break in relations with the East after the fall of Constantinople—the institution fell into oblivion. It was revived among us toward the end of the last century by one of the great “ascetics,” as they called him, Païssy Velitchkovsky, and his disciples. But to this day it exists in only a few monasteries, and in Russia it has sometimes been almost persecuted as an innovation. It flourished especially in the famous Kozelski Optin Monastery. When and how it was introduced into our monastery I cannot say. There had already been three such elders, and Zossima was the last of them. But he was almost dying of weakness and disease, and they had no one to take his place. For our monastery this was an important question, since until then it had not been distinguished by anything in particular: it had no relics of saints, no wonder-working ikons, no glorious traditions, no historical exploits. It had flourished and become famous all over Russia through its elders, and pilgrims had flocked from every part of the country, thousands of miles, to see and hear them.

What was such an elder? An elder was one who took your soul and your will into his own soul and will. When you choose an elder, you give up your own will and surrender it to him in complete submission, complete self-denial. This novitiate, this terrible school of self-denial, is taken on voluntarily, in the hope of conquering and mastering oneself, so that after a life of obedience one may reach perfect freedom—that is, freedom from self—and escape the fate of those who have lived their whole lives without finding their true selves in themselves. This institution of elders is not founded on theory. It was established in the East out of a thousand years of practice. What is owed to an elder is not the ordinary “obedience” that has always existed in our Russian monasteries. It involves confession to the elder by all who have submitted to him, and an unbreakable bond between him and them.

The story is told, for instance, that in the early days of Christianity one such novice failed to carry out some command his elder had given him. He left his monastery in Syria and went to Egypt. There, after great exploits, he was at last found worthy to suffer torture and a martyr’s death for the faith. The Church regarded him as a saint, and as they were burying him, the deacon called out, “Depart, all you unbaptized.” Suddenly the coffin with the martyr’s body left its place and was thrown out of the church. This happened three times. Only at last did they learn that this holy man had broken his vow of obedience and left his elder, and so, in spite of his great deeds, could not be forgiven without the elder’s absolution. Only after that could the funeral take place. This, of course, is only an old legend. But here is a recent instance.

A monk was suddenly ordered by his elder to leave Athos, which he loved as a sacred place and a haven of refuge. He was to go first to Jerusalem to pay homage to the Holy Places, and then to the north, to Siberia: “There is the place for you, and not here.” The monk, overwhelmed with sorrow, went to the Ecumenical Patriarch in Constantinople and begged him to release him from his obedience. But the Patriarch replied that not only was he unable to release him, but there was not and could not be any power on earth that could release him, except the elder who had himself laid that duty on him. In this way the elders are endowed, in certain cases, with unlimited and inexplicable authority. That is why in many of our monasteries the institution was at first resisted almost to the point of persecution. Meanwhile the elders at once began to be highly esteemed among the people. Crowds of ignorant people, as well as men of distinction, flocked, for instance, to the elders of our monastery to confess their doubts, their sins and their sufferings, and to ask for counsel and admonition. Seeing this, the opponents of the elders declared that the sacrament of confession was being arbitrarily and frivolously degraded, though the monk’s or layman’s continual opening of his heart to the elder had nothing of the character of the sacrament. In the end, however, the institution of elders has been kept and is becoming established in Russian monasteries. It is true, perhaps, that this instrument, which had stood the test of a thousand years for the moral regeneration of a man from slavery to freedom and to moral perfection, may be a two-edged weapon. It may lead some not to humility and complete self-control but to the most Satanic pride—that is, to bondage and not to freedom.

The elder Zossima was sixty-five. He came from a family of landowners and had been in the army in his early youth, serving in the Caucasus as an officer. No doubt he had impressed Alyosha by some peculiar quality of his soul. Alyosha lived in the elder’s cell, and the elder was very fond of him and let him wait on him. It should be noted that Alyosha was bound by no obligation and could go where he pleased and be away for whole days. He wore the monastic dress voluntarily, so as not to be different from the others. No doubt he liked doing so. Possibly his youthful imagination was deeply stirred by the power and fame of his elder. It was said that so many people had come over the years to confess their sins to Father Zossima and to beg him for words of advice and healing that he had acquired the keenest insight. From an unfamiliar face he could tell what a newcomer wanted and what was torturing his conscience. He sometimes astounded and almost alarmed his visitors by knowing their secrets before they had spoken a word.
